Consult Summary:
- Adult male with 3 days of acute diarrhea (4–5/day) with mild abdominal pain and one episode of vomiting; no blood or mucus; able to maintain oral intake. Advised oral rehydration and soft diet with return precautions.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Diarrhea for ~3 days.
- Symptom details:
  - Frequency: 4–5 times/day.
  - Consistency: Varies from watery to loose depending on time of day.
  - Associated symptoms: Mild abdominal pain; one episode of vomiting; decreased appetite; possible mild fever (“maybe a little bit”).
  - Denies: Blood in stool; mucus in stool.
  - Hydration/nutrition: Able to drink plenty; eating reduced due to appetite loss.
- Exposures/triggers:
  - No recent travel.
  - No suspicious or unusual foods reported.
- Progression: Persistent over 3 days; patient uncertain about next steps.
- Systems review (pertinent negatives): No reported signs of severe dehydration per clinician observation; no blood or mucus in stool.
- Additional unclear statement: Patient said “Mostly it’s been dry and red” (context unclear/inaudible).

Past Medical History:
- Asthma (ongoing). Current control not discussed. Using an inhaler (name unclear; see Medications).

Medications:
- Inhaler reported as “Lexapro/Laxepro” (yellow) for asthma — dose/route/frequency not documented. Conflict noted (Lexapro is typically escitalopram, not an inhaler).
- Over-the-counter medications: None taken for current symptoms.
- Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Social History:
- Recent travel: None.
- Diet: No recent unusual/suspect foods reported.
- Tobacco, alcohol, other substances: Not documented.
- Living situation/financial: Not documented.

Family History:
- Father: Hypertension; died of bowel cancer 10 years ago at age 62.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not documented.
- General: Patient appeared not dehydrated per clinician observation; no acute distress documented.
- Other systems: Not examined/documented in transcript.

Investigations:
- None performed during this consult.

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Acute diarrhea, uncomplicated (3 days; 4–5/day; no blood/mucus; able to hydrate; mild abdominal pain; one emesis)
  - Likely self-limiting.
  - Plan:
    - Hydration: Encourage increased oral fluids; use oral rehydration solution (e.g., Dioralyte) OTC to replace fluids and electrolytes.
    - Diet: Start with “soft” easily digestible foods (e.g., crackers, toast, jam); avoid dairy, meat, fish, and eggs initially.
    - Probiotics: Yogurt permitted (as probiotic), while avoiding milk.
    - Gradual reintroduction: After 48 hours without diarrhea, reintroduce boiled/mashed vegetables; then gradually resume meat/eggs/fish.
    - Red flags/when to seek care:
      - If diarrhea persists beyond 1 week or if blood appears in stool → arrange stool sample; consider need for antibiotics based on results.
      - If stool frequency increases significantly: note conflicting thresholds provided — “more than eight times/day” (initial statement) vs “about six to eight times/day” (later statement) associated with dehydration risk and possible need for hospital evaluation. Seek urgent care if frequency increases toward these ranges or if signs of dehydration develop.
    - Follow-up: Contact service if worsening, unable to maintain hydration, or red flags occur.
- Issue 2: Asthma (medication details unclear)
  - Plan:
    - Medication reconciliation required: clarify exact inhaler name/type and dosing at next opportunity.

- General Plan items:
  - Patient advised that consultation notes and instructions will be available in the app for review.

Quality checks:
● Missing/expected elements:
  - Vitals, full ROS, detailed asthma history/control, comprehensive medication list with doses/routes/frequencies, smoking/alcohol/substance use, immunization status, and baseline GI history not documented.
● Internal conflicts:
  - Threshold for concerning stool frequency: “>8/day” vs “6–8/day” linked to dehydration/hospital advice — conflict noted.
  - Asthma medication name: “Lexapro/Laxepro” (yellow inhaler) vs typical naming conventions — conflict/uncertainty noted.
  - Unclear patient statement: “Mostly it’s been dry and red” — context unclear, not incorporated into assessment.
● Transcript quality:
  - Occasional inaudible/unclear segments and interruptions; some confusion around medication name. Overall clinical content sufficient for basic assessment and advice.
